options: Environmental concerns about city center noise
To allow longer runways that the mountain-surrounded old airport couldn't accommodate
Expansion of the city over the old airport site
quiz.explanation: Quito's new Mariscal Sucre International Airport was relocated outside the city in 2013 to allow for longer runways — the previous airport in the city valley couldn't accommodate modern wide-body aircraft on high-altitude short runways.

laws.title: Right to Education and University System
laws.subtitle: Ecuador's free university education and quality challenges
laws.fullDescription: Ecuador's 2008 Constitution guaranteed free university education through public universities. This led to a significant expansion of university enrollment but also quality concerns. The SENESCYT (National Secretariat of Higher Education) administers a standardized admission exam (ENES, now Sistema de Nivelación y Admisión) determining university admission. Correa created new public universities ('Yachay' knowledge city concept). The Constitutional Court struck down some SENESCYT restrictions on university access. Private universities coexist alongside public ones. Academic freedom has been contested — researchers critical of government policies faced pressure under Correa. FLACSO and other independent academic institutions provided alternative spaces.
laws.penalty: N/A — educational framework; accreditation violations result in institutional sanctions
exceptions: Foreign students may pay fees at public universities
Graduate programs may charge enrollment fees even at public universities
Private universities set their own tuition rates

quiz.q: What system does Ecuador use for standardized university admission?
options: ENES/Sistema de Nivelación y Admisión administered by SENESCYT
quiz.explanation: Ecuador uses the ENES/Sistema de Nivelación y Admisión administered by SENESCYT (National Secretariat of Higher Education) as a standardized exam determining university admission to public universities.

laws.title: Migration Law and Darién Gap Crisis
laws.subtitle: Ecuador as origin and transit country in migration crisis
laws.fullDescription: Ecuador is both an origin country for migrants (fleeing cartel violence and economic crisis) and a transit country for Venezuelans and others heading north through the Darién Gap to the United States. Ecuador passed a relatively open Human Mobility Law (2017) providing rights to migrants and asylum seekers. However, the security crisis has strained the system. Ecuadorian migrants in the US face deportation threats. Remittances from Ecuadorians abroad are economically significant. The mass migration of Venezuelans (approximately 400,000 in Ecuador) has tested the system. Ecuador has cooperated with IOM and UNHCR on migration management.
laws.penalty: Administrative detention and deportation for unauthorized entry; criminal prosecution for migrant smuggling
exceptions: 1951 Refugee Convention protections apply to asylum seekers
Venezuela temporary protection status mechanisms provide relief
Unaccompanied minors receive special protections under the Human Mobility Law

quiz.q: Approximately how many Venezuelans are in Ecuador?
quiz.explanation: Approximately 400,000 Venezuelans are in Ecuador — a significant population that has tested Ecuador's relatively open Human Mobility Law system and strained public services, though many use Ecuador as transit to other destinations.

laws.title: Shrimp Industry and Aquaculture Law
laws.subtitle: Ecuador's major shrimp export sector
laws.fullDescription: Ecuador is one of the world's top shrimp exporters, with the industry concentrated in coastal Guayas and El Oro provinces. The shrimp farming industry (camaronicultura) transformed coastal mangrove ecosystems — significant mangrove destruction for shrimp ponds occurred in the 1980s-90s before environmental regulations tightened. The aquaculture law requires environmental permits and prohibits new mangrove destruction. Shrimp exports (primarily white leg shrimp, Litopenaeus vannamei) exceed $4 billion annually. COVID-19 created demand disruptions. China and Europe are major markets. Disease outbreaks (Early Mortality Syndrome, white spot disease) periodically hit the industry.
laws.penalty: Fines and licence revocation for mangrove destruction; criminal prosecution for illegal aquaculture expansion
exceptions: Existing shrimp ponds predating regulations may continue operating under remediation agreements
Certified sustainable aquaculture operations qualify for premium market access
Research aquaculture with university authorization has different permitting

quiz.q: Approximately what do Ecuador's annual shrimp exports amount to?
quiz.explanation: Ecuador's shrimp exports exceed $4 billion annually, making it one of the world's top shrimp exporters with the industry concentrated in coastal provinces — though it has caused significant historical mangrove destruction.

laws.title: Witness Protection and Anti-Impunity Law
laws.subtitle: Ecuador's protection of witnesses in major criminal cases
laws.fullDescription: Ecuador's Fiscalía General operates a witness and victim protection program under the Organic Law on Victims and Witnesses. Given the cartel crisis, witness protection has become critical — witnesses to organized crime face severe retaliation risks. Prosecutors have used protected witnesses to build cases against gang leadership. The assassination of presidential candidate Villavicencio (himself a former journalist who had received threats) highlighted the inadequacy of protection programs. Ecuador cooperates internationally for witness relocation. Key cases — prison massacres, cartel operations, corruption — depend on protected witnesses. The program is chronically underfunded relative to need.
laws.penalty: N/A — protective program; threatening or harming witnesses subject to enhanced criminal penalties
exceptions: Certain witnesses may testify via videoconference or with identity concealment
Children witness to crimes have additional protections
International witnesses may testify under bilateral judicial cooperation agreements

quiz.q: What high-profile event highlighted inadequacies in Ecuador's witness and protection programs?
options: Assassination of presidential candidate Fernando Villavicencio despite receiving threats
quiz.explanation: The assassination of presidential candidate Fernando Villavicencio — despite his having received cartel threats and sought protection — highlighted critical inadequacies in Ecuador's witness and person protection programs.

laws.title: Mangrove Protection Law
laws.subtitle: Ecuador's legal framework protecting coastal mangroves
laws.fullDescription: Ecuador lost over 70% of its mangrove forests between 1970 and 1998 primarily to shrimp aquaculture expansion. The Mangrove Protection Law and subsequent regulations prohibit new mangrove clearing and mandate restoration where possible. Mangroves provide critical ecosystem services — coastal protection, fish nurseries, carbon sequestration. The Ministry of Environment has worked with shrimp industry and coastal communities on mangrove recovery programs. Ecuador's remaining mangroves are primarily in Esmeraldas and Manabí provinces. International conservation funding supports mangrove restoration. Climate change and sea level rise threaten remaining mangroves.
laws.penalty: Criminal prosecution for mangrove destruction; environmental remediation orders; fines
exceptions: Existing aquaculture operations predating prohibition may continue with monitoring
Subsistence fishing communities may access mangroves for traditional fishing
Scientific research in mangrove areas permitted with authorization

quiz.q: What percentage of Ecuador's mangrove forests were lost between 1970 and 1998?
quiz.explanation: Ecuador lost over 70% of its mangrove forests between 1970 and 1998, primarily due to expansion of shrimp aquaculture, leading to strict legal protections against further destruction.

laws.title: Transparency and Access to Information Law
laws.subtitle: Ecuador's framework for government transparency
laws.fullDescription: Ecuador's Organic Law of Transparency and Access to Public Information (LOTAIP) requires public institutions to publish information online and respond to access to information requests within 10 days. The Defensoría del Pueblo (Ombudsman) enforces compliance. Despite the law, government responsiveness varies significantly — particularly for sensitive security and economic information. The Correa government was criticized for selectively releasing information while legally complying with LOTAIP requirements. The security crisis has been used to justify withholding information as security-sensitive. Civil society organizations use LOTAIP extensively to monitor government contracting and social programs.
laws.penalty: Fines for officials who obstruct information access; habeas data action available for personal data requests
exceptions: National security information may be classified and withheld
Personal data of individuals protected from disclosure
Ongoing criminal investigations information withheld until case resolution

quiz.q: How many days does Ecuador's LOTAIP law require public institutions to respond to information requests?
quiz.explanation: Ecuador's LOTAIP (Organic Law of Transparency and Access to Public Information) requires public institutions to respond to access to information requests within 10 days, with the Defensoría del Pueblo enforcing compliance.

laws.title: Tourism Law and Ecotourism Regulation
laws.subtitle: Ecuador's tourism framework including Galápagos
laws.fullDescription: Tourism is a major economic sector in Ecuador, particularly ecotourism to the Galápagos, Amazon, and Andean regions. The Tourism Law requires operators to be licensed through the Ministry of Tourism. Galápagos tourism is strictly regulated — visitor numbers are controlled, all tourists must travel with licensed naturalist guides, and park fees fund conservation. The Galápagos has approximately 300,000 visitors annually. Community-based ecotourism in the Amazon has grown, providing income for indigenous communities while protecting forests. COVID-19 devastated the tourism sector in 2020–2021. The security crisis from 2022 onwards has affected tourist numbers, particularly in formerly safe coastal and urban destinations.
laws.penalty: Fines for unlicensed tourism operations; Galápagos National Park violations can result in deportation from islands
exceptions: Community ecotourism operations have simplified registration in some provinces
Scientific research expeditions not classified as tourism
Diplomatic visitors to Galápagos have separate entry protocols

quiz.q: Approximately how many visitors does the Galápagos receive annually?
quiz.explanation: The Galápagos Islands receive approximately 300,000 visitors annually under a strictly controlled system requiring licensed naturalist guides, with park fees funding conservation of one of the world's most unique ecosystems.

laws.title: Juvenile Justice System
laws.subtitle: Ecuador's legal framework for juvenile offenders
laws.fullDescription: Ecuador's Childhood and Adolescence Code (2003) governs juvenile justice. Adolescents aged 12–17 who commit offenses are subject to the juvenile system, not adult criminal law. Penalties are reformative rather than punitive — maximum detention periods are significantly shorter than adult sentences. The cartel crisis has involved recruitment of minors into gangs — a complex legal challenge given protective intent of the juvenile system. A 2023 legislative reform increased juvenile penalties for serious crimes involving minors in criminal organizations. Juvenile detention centers (Centros de Adolescentes Infractores) have faced overcrowding. Rehabilitation programs with educational and vocational components are mandated.
laws.penalty: Maximum 4–8 years socio-educational measures for serious offenses by adolescents; shorter for less serious
exceptions: Adolescents who commit offenses after turning 18 tried as adults for acts after that date
Serious international crimes may have special provisions
Children under 12 cannot be held criminally responsible under any circumstances

quiz.q: What is the focus of Ecuador's juvenile justice system for offending adolescents?
quiz.explanation: Ecuador's juvenile justice system under the Childhood and Adolescence Code focuses on reformative and rehabilitative rather than punitive measures for offending adolescents, with mandated educational and vocational components.

laws.title: Industrial Policy and Manufacturing Development
laws.subtitle: Ecuador's efforts to diversify beyond primary commodities
laws.fullDescription: Ecuador's economy is heavily dependent on primary commodity exports — oil, bananas, shrimp, flowers, and cocoa. The government has attempted industrial policy to add value to these commodities (e.g., the raw lithium export ban model from neighboring Bolivia) and develop new industries. The MIPRO (Ministry of Production) promotes domestic manufacturing through tariff protection and investment incentives. Special Economic Zones (Zonas Especiales de Desarrollo Económico — ZEDE) offer tax incentives. However, Ecuador's small market size and high production costs (dollar-denominated wages) make industrial competitiveness challenging. The Manta-Manaos multimodal corridor aimed to attract logistics investment.
laws.penalty: N/A — industrial promotion framework; specific violations under customs and tax law
exceptions: ZEDE companies have tax and labour regulation differences from standard firms
Export industries receive drawback of import duties on inputs
Micro and small enterprises have simplified regulatory requirements

quiz.q: What key challenge does Ecuador's dollar-denominated economy create for manufacturing competitiveness?
options: High production costs from dollar wages that cannot be devalued
quiz.explanation: Ecuador's dollarized economy means wages are dollar-denominated and cannot be devalued to improve competitiveness — making manufacturing more expensive relative to countries that can devalue their currencies.

laws.title: Food Sovereignty Law
laws.subtitle: Ecuador's constitutional food sovereignty framework
laws.fullDescription: Ecuador's 2008 Constitution enshrined food sovereignty (soberanía alimentaria) — the right of peoples to define their own food and agricultural systems — as a state goal. The Organic Law on Food Sovereignty (2009) followed, establishing the Conference on Food Sovereignty as an oversight body. The law promotes agroecology, traditional seed systems, and small farmer rights. It restricts GMO crops (Ecuador is a major opponent of GMOs in agriculture). The banana and shrimp industries' dependence on monocultures and chemical inputs creates tension with food sovereignty principles. Indigenous communities' traditional seed systems are specifically protected.
laws.penalty: Fines for GMO crop introduction without authorization; regulations against seed monopolies
exceptions: Research institutions may conduct controlled GMO studies with authorization
Biofortified crops (vitamin-enhanced traditional varieties) treated differently from GM crops
Emergency food shortage situations may allow temporary exceptions

quiz.q: What agricultural technology does Ecuador's Food Sovereignty Law restrict?
quiz.explanation: Ecuador's Food Sovereignty Law restricts GMO crops, reflecting the constitution's food sovereignty principles — a position that creates tension with the banana and shrimp industries' use of monoculture agricultural systems.

laws.title: Femicide and Gender Violence Courts
laws.subtitle: Ecuador's specialized courts for gender-based violence
laws.fullDescription: Ecuador established specialized Unidades Judiciales Especializadas de Violencia contra la Mujer y la Familia (Specialized Judicial Units for Violence Against Women and Family) in major cities. These courts provide one-stop justice including protection orders, prosecution, and victim support services. The DINAPEN (National Directorate for Children and Adolescents Police) handles child protection. Despite specialized courts, femicide rates have not significantly declined. Prosecutors argue that low reporting rates — women fear retaliation or do not trust the system — and high conviction reversal rates on appeal undermine deterrence. Victim advocacy organizations support survivors through the system.
laws.penalty: Protection orders within 24 hours; femicide 22–26 years; partner violence 30 days to 3 years depending on severity
exceptions: Traditional indigenous justice may address domestic violence with court oversight
Mediation permitted for lower-level partner violence but not femicide or serious violence
Protection orders enforceable through police without additional hearing

quiz.q: What do Ecuador's specialized Unidades Judiciales Especializadas provide as a 'one-stop' service?
options: Medical, legal, and police services combined
Protection orders, prosecution, and victim support services
Housing, legal aid, and police protection
Financial assistance, legal advice, and shelter
quiz.explanation: Ecuador's specialized gender violence courts provide protection orders, prosecution, and victim support services in a one-stop model — designed to reduce barriers to justice for women experiencing violence.

laws.title: Organic Agriculture and Certification Law
laws.subtitle: Ecuador's promotion of organic and sustainable agriculture
laws.fullDescription: Ecuador has significant potential for organic agriculture given its biodiversity, climate zones, and traditional farming practices. The MAGAP (Ministry of Agriculture) and Agrocalidad regulate organic certification. Ecuador exports organic bananas, cocoa, quinoa, and coffee with organic premiums benefiting small farmers. Fair Trade and Rainforest Alliance certifications operate alongside government certification. The constitution's food sovereignty provisions and Rights of Nature support organic approaches. Community-supported agriculture networks link urban consumers with organic producers. Despite potential, organic agriculture represents a small fraction of total production due to certification costs and technical assistance gaps.
laws.penalty: Fines for false organic labeling; licence revocation for certification fraud
exceptions: Traditional indigenous farming methods may qualify for simplified organic certification
Community agricultural organizations can certify collectively
Export organic certification may be handled through bilateral recognition agreements with buyer-country certification bodies

quiz.q: What internationally known products does Ecuador export as certified organic?
quiz.explanation: Ecuador exports certified organic bananas, cocoa, quinoa, and coffee — products that receive price premiums in international markets and provide income benefits to small farmers.

laws.title: Ombudsman (Defensoría del Pueblo) and Human Rights
laws.subtitle: Ecuador's human rights protection institution
laws.fullDescription: Ecuador's Defensoría del Pueblo (Ombudsman) is a constitutionally mandated institution for human rights protection, LOTAIP enforcement, and public service oversight. The Defensoría investigates human rights complaints, mediates disputes between citizens and state, and monitors detention conditions. Under Correa, the Defensoría's independence was questioned — the head was seen as politically aligned. The 2013 constitution strengthened the CPCCS oversight of the Defensoría's appointment. During the security crisis, the Defensoría documented prison conditions and deaths. The Defensoría also handles migrant rights, environmental rights, and children's rights cases.
laws.penalty: N/A — human rights investigation body; its recommendations are not legally binding but can trigger legal proceedings
exceptions: Defensoría cannot prosecute — it refers cases to Fiscalía
Some categories of state security matters outside Defensoría jurisdiction
International cooperation allows Defensoría to work with Inter-American Commission

quiz.q: What is a key limitation of Ecuador's Defensoría del Pueblo?
options: It can only handle migration cases
Its recommendations are not legally binding — it can only refer cases to prosecutors
quiz.explanation: Ecuador's Defensoría del Pueblo cannot prosecute — its recommendations are not legally binding, and it must refer cases to the Fiscalía for prosecution — limiting its enforcement power despite its constitutional mandate.

laws.title: Social Housing and Slum Upgrading
laws.subtitle: Ecuador's housing programs for vulnerable populations
laws.fullDescription: Ecuador's MIDUVI administers housing subsidy programs targeting low-income families. The 'Casa para Todos' (Home for All) program under Correa built hundreds of thousands of units. Subsidies help families access mortgages through the BIESS (social security bank) or private banks. The informal 'suburbios' of Guayaquil represent a major urban land challenge — regularization programs have provided titles to some informal settlers. The 2016 earthquake destroyed thousands of homes in Manabí, requiring emergency reconstruction. Rural housing programs focus on improving indigenous and rural community housing with locally appropriate designs.
laws.penalty: N/A — housing subsidy framework; construction fraud in government housing programs subject to criminal prosecution
exceptions: Disaster-affected households receive priority and simplified process
Indigenous communities can receive housing support using traditional construction materials
Elderly and disabled persons receive priority allocation

quiz.q: What social security institution provides mortgage financing for Ecuador's housing subsidy program beneficiaries?
quiz.explanation: Ecuador's BIESS (social security bank connected to IESS) provides mortgage financing for housing subsidy program beneficiaries, linking social security savings to affordable housing access.

laws.title: Anti-Money Laundering and Financial Intelligence
laws.subtitle: Ecuador's financial crime prevention framework
laws.fullDescription: Ecuador's Financial and Economic Analysis Unit (UAFE) coordinates anti-money laundering efforts under the Organic Law for Prevention, Detection and Eradication of Money Laundering. Financial institutions, real estate agents, and lawyers handling transactions must report suspicious activities. The drug trafficking crisis has dramatically increased money laundering risks — cartel profits enter Ecuador's dollar economy through real estate, transportation, and food businesses. Ecuador was placed on FATF grey list in 2019 but removed in 2022 after implementing reforms. International cooperation with US, Colombia, and European financial intelligence units is significant.
laws.penalty: 4–8 years imprisonment for money laundering; asset forfeiture; fines for reporting institution failures
exceptions: Small financial transactions below threshold not subject to reporting requirements
Professional activities protected by lawyer-client privilege have limited carve-outs
Currency exchange below threshold not subject to full identification requirements

quiz.q: When was Ecuador removed from the FATF grey list?
quiz.explanation: Ecuador was removed from the FATF grey list in 2022 after implementing anti-money laundering reforms — a significant step for its financial sector reputation, having been placed on the list in 2019.

laws.title: Climate Change Law and INDC
laws.subtitle: Ecuador's climate commitments and vulnerability
laws.fullDescription: Ecuador is highly vulnerable to climate change despite contributing minimally to global emissions. The Andes glaciers are retreating — affecting water supply to highland cities. Coastal regions face sea level rise. El Niño events are intensifying — causing droughts reducing hydroelectric capacity and floods affecting coastal agriculture. Ecuador ratified the Paris Agreement and submitted NDCs (Nationally Determined Contributions) targeting 20–25% emissions reduction. The Yasuní referendum reflected a public willingness to sacrifice oil revenue for climate reasons. Ecuador participates in the Amazon cooperation framework (ACTO). The 2024 energy crisis from hydroelectric drought damage demonstrated concrete climate vulnerability.
laws.penalty: N/A — climate policy; environmental violations under separate law
exceptions: Developing country flexibility provisions apply to Ecuador's NDCs
Loss and damage financing from developed countries sought for extreme events
Carbon market mechanisms allow international offset purchases

quiz.q: What major infrastructure crisis in 2024 demonstrated Ecuador's concrete climate vulnerability?
options: Coastal flooding from sea level rise
Energy crisis from hydroelectric drought reducing dam output
quiz.explanation: Ecuador's 2024 energy crisis, caused by drought reducing water levels in hydroelectric dams (particularly Coca Codo Sinclair), demonstrated concrete climate vulnerability — forcing 10-14 hour daily blackouts nationwide.

laws.title: Digital Rights and Data Protection
laws.subtitle: Ecuador's personal data protection framework
laws.fullDescription: Following the massive 2019 Novaestrat data breach exposing virtually all Ecuadorians' personal information, Ecuador enacted the Organic Personal Data Protection Law (2021). The law created the Data Protection Authority (Superintendencia de Protección de Datos Personales), establishes consent requirements for data processing, grants rights to access, rectify, and delete personal data, and requires security measures for data processors. The law aligns with GDPR principles. Implementation is ongoing — businesses have adaptation timelines. Government agencies must also comply. The intersection of data protection and the security apparatus' surveillance powers creates ongoing tensions.
laws.penalty: Fines of $100–$200,000 for data protection violations; enhanced penalties for sensitive data breaches
exceptions: National security and intelligence data processing exempt from civilian oversight
Journalistic and research purposes may qualify for public interest exceptions
Historical archives and research databases have different compliance timelines
laws.sourceLabel: Superintendencia de Protección de Datos Ecuador

quiz.q: What event in 2019 prompted Ecuador to enact comprehensive data protection legislation?
options: The Novaestrat data breach exposing virtually all Ecuadorians' personal information
quiz.explanation: The 2019 Novaestrat data breach exposing the personal data of approximately 17 million Ecuadorians (nearly the entire population) prompted Ecuador to enact the Organic Personal Data Protection Law in 2021.

laws.title: Inter-American Court of Human Rights and Ecuador
laws.subtitle: Ecuador's international human rights accountability
laws.fullDescription: Ecuador has been subject to numerous rulings from the Inter-American Court of Human Rights (IACtHR). Landmark cases include Sarayaku vs. Ecuador (2012 — indigenous consultation rights), Chaparro Álvarez vs. Ecuador (arbitrary detention), and cases involving journalists prosecuted by Correa. Ecuador generally complies with IACHR precautionary measures and IACtHR rulings. The Inter-American Commission has been active in monitoring Ecuador's security crisis including prison massacres. The IACHR granted precautionary measures for prison populations at risk. Ecuador's acceptance of IACtHR jurisdiction in 1984 provides an important external accountability mechanism.
laws.penalty: N/A — international obligation; Ecuador pays reparations ordered by IACtHR
exceptions: State sovereignty limits but does not eliminate IACtHR jurisdiction
Some national security measures reviewed under different standards
Diplomatic immunity not applicable to IACtHR proceedings

quiz.q: What did the IACtHR rule in the landmark Sarayaku vs. Ecuador case?
options: Oil drilling in Sarayaku territory was legal
Ecuador violated the Kichwa Sarayaku community's right to prior consultation regarding oil exploration
Sarayaku had no land rights under international law
The Rights of Nature applied to Sarayaku territory
quiz.explanation: In the landmark 2012 Sarayaku vs. Ecuador case, the IACtHR ruled that Ecuador violated the Kichwa Sarayaku community's right to free, prior, and informed consultation by allowing oil exploration in their territory without proper consultation.

laws.title: Cocoa and Chocolate Industry Regulation
laws.subtitle: Ecuador's fine cocoa sector and value chain
laws.fullDescription: Ecuador produces approximately 65% of the world's fine aroma cocoa (Arriba/Nacional variety), a premium product used by luxury chocolate makers globally. The cocoa sector employs hundreds of thousands of small farmers, particularly in coastal and Amazon regions. Agrocalidad certifies cocoa quality and manages phytosanitary standards for export. Ecuador has actively promoted value addition — moving from exporting raw cocoa beans to processed cocoa products and artisan chocolate. The Ministerio de Producción supports the cacao-chocolate value chain. International buyers including Swiss and Belgian luxury chocolatiers source primarily from Ecuador. Climate change and disease (monilia fungus) threaten cocoa production.
laws.penalty: Export fines for substandard cocoa violating quality certification; agricultural support conditions tied to compliance
exceptions: Small farmer cooperatives have simplified certification processes
Organic and fair trade certified cocoa follows independent certification standards
Research institutions may work with non-standard cocoa varieties

quiz.q: What percentage of the world's fine aroma cocoa does Ecuador produce?
quiz.explanation: Ecuador produces approximately 65% of the world's fine aroma cocoa (Arriba/Nacional variety), making it the dominant global supplier of premium cocoa used by luxury chocolate manufacturers.

laws.title: Correa Conviction and Exile — Legal Implications
laws.subtitle: Former president's corruption conviction and its political impact
laws.fullDescription: Former President Rafael Correa was convicted in absentia by an Ecuadorian court in April 2020 in the Sobornos (bribes) case, sentenced to 8 years imprisonment and barred from public office for 25 years. The case involved systematic collection of political contributions from companies receiving government contracts — money funneled to Correa's RC movement. Correa, residing in Belgium, contests the verdict as politically motivated. Ecuador requested extradition but Belgium declined, citing political nature of charges. Correa's political movement (now Revolución Ciudadana) continues actively — his ally Luisa González nearly won the 2023 election. The case has polarized Ecuador between Correa supporters and opponents.
laws.penalty: 8 years imprisonment (in absentia); 25-year bar from public office; asset confiscation
exceptions: Correa contests jurisdiction and fairness of the in absentia trial
Inter-American Commission has received complaints about the trial's impartiality
Political asylum in Belgium provides protection from extradition

quiz.q: How long is Correa barred from public office following his conviction?
quiz.explanation: Rafael Correa was barred from holding public office for 25 years following his 2020 in absentia conviction in the Sobornos case — in addition to the 8-year prison sentence he would face if he returned to Ecuador.

laws.title: Indigenous Land Rights — CONAIE and Territorial Conflict
laws.subtitle: Ongoing conflicts over indigenous territories
laws.fullDescription: Ecuador's indigenous nationalities — particularly Amazon groups including Waorani, Achuar, Kichwa, Shuar, and Huaorani — face continuing territorial threats from oil, mining, and agricultural expansion. CONAIE (Confederation of Indigenous Nationalities of Ecuador) has organized national strikes (paros nacionales) that have paralyzed Ecuador multiple times — in 2022, an 18-day strike brought the economy to a halt, forcing negotiations with President Lasso. The strikes reflect frustration over living costs, lack of consultation, and territorial insecurity. Constitutional protections for indigenous territories are formally strong but enforcement is weak. The ILO Convention 169 requires free prior informed consent for resource extraction.
laws.penalty: N/A — land rights framework; illegal incursion on titled indigenous territory criminally prosecuted
exceptions: Pre-existing oil contracts on overlapping areas create legal complexity
Infrastructure projects deemed national interest may proceed with modified consultation
Environmental and territorial rights must be balanced in court determinations

quiz.q: In 2022, how long did CONAIE's national strike last that paralyzed Ecuador?
quiz.explanation: CONAIE's 2022 national strike (paro nacional) lasted 18 days, paralyzed Ecuador's economy, and forced negotiations with President Lasso over living costs, consultation rights, and indigenous territorial security.

laws.title: Freedom of Assembly and Social Protest Law
laws.subtitle: Ecuador's legal framework for demonstrations
laws.fullDescription: Ecuador's constitution guarantees the right to peaceful assembly and protest. The 2021 Law of Humanitarian Support provided some protest framework, but security forces use of force during protests has been documented. The 2019 protests against fuel subsidy removal — which forced Correa-era austerity measures — saw security forces use tear gas and rubber bullets. The 2022 indigenous strikes similarly faced security force response. Protest permit requirements exist but are generally not enforced for peaceful marches. The government has used state of exception powers to restrict movement during strikes. International human rights bodies have criticized disproportionate use of force against protesters.
laws.penalty: Fines for blocking roads (sabotaje y terrorismo charges sometimes applied); up to 3 years for violent protesters
exceptions: Peaceful marches generally permitted without prior authorization
Political party events require minimal notification
Workers' strikes on public property subject to different rules than civil demonstrations

quiz.q: What did Ecuador's 2019 protests that paralyzed Quito concern?
options: Removal of fuel subsidies under IMF-backed austerity
quiz.explanation: Ecuador's major 2019 protests that paralyzed Quito concerned the removal of fuel subsidies as part of IMF-backed austerity measures — demonstrations that forced the government to temporarily relocate to Guayaquil.

laws.title: El Niño Preparedness and Coastal Flood Law
laws.subtitle: Ecuador's legal framework for climate-driven disasters
laws.fullDescription: Ecuador is severely affected by El Niño weather events — the 1997–98 El Niño caused $2.9 billion in damage. Coastal flooding, landslides, and river overflow affect Manabí, Guayas, and El Oro provinces most severely. The Secretaría de Gestión de Riesgos manages preparedness and response. Early warning systems for coastal flooding include sensor networks on major rivers. Building codes in flood-prone areas require elevation requirements. The 2023–24 El Niño again caused significant flooding and agricultural damage while simultaneously reducing Andean rainfall for hydroelectric generation. Climate change is intensifying El Niño events.
laws.penalty: N/A — disaster management framework; construction violations in flood zones subject to demolition and fines
exceptions: Emergency reconstruction after flood disaster may use simplified permitting
Farmers in flood zones receive agricultural insurance through AgroSeguro
Mobile homes and temporary structures in flood zones have different standards
laws.sourceLabel: Secretaría de Gestión de Riesgos Ecuador

quiz.q: How much damage did the 1997–98 El Niño event cause in Ecuador?
quiz.explanation: The 1997–98 El Niño event caused approximately $2.9 billion in damage in Ecuador, affecting coastal provinces with flooding, landslides, and agricultural destruction — one of the worst natural disasters in Ecuador's recent history.

laws.title: Julian Assange and Ecuador's Asylum Policy
laws.subtitle: Ecuador's grant and revocation of asylum to Assange
laws.fullDescription: Ecuador granted asylum to WikiLeaks founder Julian Assange in August 2012 when he entered Ecuador's London embassy to avoid extradition to Sweden. President Correa defended Assange as a persecuted journalist. Assange lived in the embassy for nearly 7 years. In April 2019, President Moreno withdrew Assange's asylum and citizenship, citing behavior violations — allowing British police to arrest him. Critics accused Moreno of complying with US and UK pressure. The case raised major questions about Ecuador's asylum and refugee law, diplomatic relations, and freedom of expression. Assange's legal battle continued in UK courts until his plea deal with the US in 2024.
laws.penalty: N/A — diplomatic asylum policy; Ecuador' sovereignty over embassy area created unique legal situation
exceptions: Diplomatic premises have special status under Vienna Convention on Diplomatic Relations
Asylum withdrawal requires formal revocation process
International refugee law protections apply to recognized asylum seekers

quiz.q: How many years did Julian Assange live in Ecuador's London embassy after being granted asylum?
quiz.explanation: Julian Assange lived in Ecuador's London embassy for nearly 7 years (2012–2019) after being granted asylum by President Correa, until President Moreno withdrew the asylum and allowed British police to arrest him.

laws.title: Cultural Heritage Law and National Identity
laws.subtitle: Ecuador's cultural heritage protection
laws.fullDescription: Ecuador's rich cultural heritage encompasses pre-Columbian indigenous cultures (Valdivia, Chorrera, Tolita, Caranqui), colonial Spanish architecture, and living indigenous traditions. The Ministry of Culture administers cultural heritage policy. Quito's Historic Center is one of the best-preserved Spanish colonial cities in the Americas and a UNESCO World Heritage Site. The Organic Culture Law protects intangible cultural heritage including indigenous ceremonies, traditional knowledge, and music. Ecuador's film industry receives state support. Cultural spaces (Casa de la Cultura Ecuatoriana) exist across the country. Illegal export of archaeological objects is criminalized.
laws.penalty: Fines and imprisonment for heritage site damage and archaeological object trafficking
exceptions: Temporary cultural exchanges and museum loans under bilateral agreements permitted
Academic archaeological research with authorization can excavate
Traditional artisans may sell traditional crafts including replicas under fair use

quiz.q: What UNESCO recognition does Quito's Historic Center hold?
options: One of the best-preserved Spanish colonial cities and World Heritage Site
quiz.explanation: Quito's Historic Center is one of the best-preserved Spanish colonial cities in the Americas and holds UNESCO World Heritage Site status — a major tourism attraction and focus of Ecuador's cultural heritage protection.

laws.title: Wiretapping and Surveillance Law
laws.subtitle: Ecuador's legal framework for electronic surveillance
laws.fullDescription: Ecuador's COIP (2014) includes provisions on legal interception of communications requiring judicial authorization. The intelligence services (Secretaría de Inteligencia — SENAIN) have surveillance powers under the National Intelligence Law. Under Correa, the surveillance of journalists, opposition politicians, and civil society was extensively documented — the 'caso espionaje' revealed systematic monitoring. The National Police's Unidad de Investigación Cibernética handles digital forensics for criminal investigations. Ecuador cooperates with US DEA and intelligence agencies on drug trafficking surveillance. Post-Correa reforms attempted to improve oversight but the security crisis has justified expanded surveillance.
laws.penalty: Criminal prosecution for unauthorized wiretapping; judicial oversight required for legitimate interception
exceptions: Judicial-authorized wiretapping for criminal investigations legal
Intelligence operations against terrorism and organized crime may have expedited authorization
International intelligence cooperation under bilateral agreements has different oversight

quiz.q: What term refers to the surveillance scandal revealed under President Correa?
quiz.explanation: The 'caso espionaje' (espionage case) revealed systematic government surveillance of journalists, opposition politicians, and civil society under President Correa — documenting the intelligence services' monitoring of government critics.

laws.title: Public-Private Partnerships and Concession Law
laws.subtitle: Ecuador's framework for infrastructure concessions
laws.fullDescription: Ecuador's Organic Law on Public-Private Partnerships (APP Law, 2015/amended) enables private investment in public infrastructure through concession contracts. The SENPLADES (National Planning Secretariat) coordinates public investment planning including PPPs. Concession contracts for ports, airports, and toll roads have been developed. The Quito metro project involved international financing and private construction. Under the IMF program, Ecuador was encouraged to expand PPP use to reduce public fiscal burden. Transparency requirements for PPP contracts improved after Odebrecht scandal. Chinese companies participate in some infrastructure concessions.
laws.penalty: N/A — investment framework; contract violations subject to arbitration
exceptions: Strategic sectors (oil, water, electricity) have restrictions on full privatization
Social infrastructure (hospitals, schools) PPPs have service quality guarantees
Emergency infrastructure bypasses standard PPP tender process

quiz.q: What major infrastructure project in Quito involved international financing and private construction?
quiz.explanation: The Quito metro project involved international financing and private construction contracts — a major urban infrastructure investment that brought modern mass transit to Ecuador's capital city.

laws.title: Human Trafficking Law
laws.subtitle: Ecuador's anti-trafficking framework
laws.fullDescription: Ecuador's COIP (2014) criminalizes human trafficking for labor exploitation, sexual exploitation, and organ trafficking. Ecuador is a source, transit, and destination country for trafficking. Colombian and Venezuelan migrants are vulnerable in transit. Domestic trafficking for labor in mines, agriculture, and domestic service affects women and children. Sexual trafficking occurs in tourist areas. The Anti-Trafficking Unit of the National Police works with the Fiscalía on prosecutions. Ecuador cooperates with IOM on victim assistance programs. The Victim and Witness Protection Program provides support. US State Department TIP reports have noted improvements in Ecuador's anti-trafficking efforts.
laws.penalty: 13–16 years for human trafficking; enhanced penalties for trafficking children and organ trafficking
exceptions: Victims of trafficking are protected from prosecution for crimes committed as a result of being trafficked
Child victims receive specialized shelter and services
International cooperation for victim repatriation under bilateral agreements

quiz.q: What makes Ecuador distinctive in human trafficking geography?
options: It is only an origin country
It is only a destination country
It is a source, transit, and destination country
It only experiences international trafficking, not domestic
quiz.explanation: Ecuador is a source, transit, and destination country for human trafficking — a triple role reflecting its geographic position between Colombia and Peru, its tourism sector, and vulnerable migrant populations passing through.

laws.title: Amazon Protection and ACTO Framework
laws.subtitle: Ecuador's Amazon conservation commitments
laws.fullDescription: Ecuador's Amazon (Amazonía) covers approximately 37% of the country's territory and is among the world's most biodiverse regions. The Amazonian territories of the Napo, Pastaza, Morona Santiago, Sucumbíos, and Orellana provinces contain significant uncontacted indigenous peoples, extraordinary biodiversity, and oil reserves. Ecuador participates in the Amazon Cooperation Treaty Organization (ACTO). The 2019 Declaration of Leticia committed Amazon countries to strengthened forest protection. Despite commitments, oil extraction in the Amazon (particularly Block 43/ITT) and gold mining expansion have continued. Community forest management with indigenous groups is promoted.
laws.penalty: Criminal prosecution for illegal deforestation; injunctions under Rights of Nature for ecosystem destruction
exceptions: Pre-existing oil contracts create ongoing extraction rights subject to renegotiation
Indigenous community forest management may involve selective extraction
Scientific monitoring permits allow presence in otherwise restricted areas

quiz.q: What percentage of Ecuador's territory is covered by the Amazon?
quiz.explanation: Ecuador's Amazon covers approximately 37% of the country's territory, containing extraordinary biodiversity, uncontacted indigenous peoples, and significant oil reserves — making conservation-versus-extraction tradeoffs central to Ecuadorian policy.

laws.title: Prison Reform and Human Rights in Detention
laws.subtitle: Ecuador's reform efforts following the prison crisis
laws.fullDescription: Following the 2021 prison massacres killing over 316 inmates, Ecuador undertook prison reform measures including military deployment in prisons, construction of new maximum security facilities, and cell phone signal blocking. The Organic Law on the Execution of Sentences and Penitentiary Rehabilitation provides the framework for prison management. Ecuador's prison population had grown dramatically with anti-cartel crackdowns. Overcrowding (prisons operating at 200–300% capacity) remains a structural problem. The SNAI (National Service for Comprehensive Attention to Adults Deprived of Liberty) manages the prison system. International organizations documented continuing violence even after military deployment.
laws.penalty: N/A — prison management framework; officials responsible for prison conditions subject to disciplinary action
exceptions: Pre-trial detainees must be held separately from convicted prisoners
Women with young children have special housing provisions
Medical care must be provided regardless of security status

quiz.q: At what capacity were Ecuador's prisons operating at the time of the 2021 massacres?
quiz.explanation: Ecuador's prisons were operating at 200–300% of their intended capacity during the 2021 prison massacres — extreme overcrowding that made the facilities ungovernable and allowed cartels to operate criminal enterprises from inside.

laws.title: IMF Program and Fiscal Adjustment
laws.subtitle: Ecuador's relationship with the IMF and fiscal constraints
laws.fullDescription: Ecuador signed a $4.2 billion Extended Fund Facility agreement with the IMF in 2019 under President Moreno, requiring fiscal adjustment including reducing fuel subsidies. The 2019 protests forced renegotiation. COVID-19 derailed the program. Ecuador subsequently negotiated a new $6.5 billion IMF program in 2021 under President Lasso. The programs require reducing the fiscal deficit, reforming public enterprises, and improving tax collection. Ecuador's debt restructuring in 2020 achieved $1.7 billion in savings. The security crisis created competing fiscal demands — military and police expansion vs. fiscal consolidation. Ecuador's fiscal space is severely constrained by dollarization (no monetary policy) and weak growth.
laws.penalty: N/A — international financial framework; domestic law must align with program commitments
exceptions: Social spending floors protect minimum social program expenditure
Emergency spending (natural disasters, security) may be outside standard fiscal rules
Climate finance from multilateral sources supplements fiscal capacity

quiz.q: How much did Ecuador's 2020 debt restructuring save?
quiz.explanation: Ecuador's 2020 debt restructuring achieved approximately $1.7 billion in savings, providing fiscal relief during the COVID-19 crisis when economic activity collapsed and oil revenues fell sharply.

laws.title: State of Exception — Constitutional Review
laws.subtitle: Ecuador's Constitutional Court oversight of emergency powers
laws.fullDescription: Ecuador's Constitutional Court has actively reviewed declarations of state of exception, sometimes striking down parts of them or requiring reporting. In 2024, the Court reviewed Noboa's anti-cartel emergency declarations and upheld the core military deployment while requiring additional oversight measures. The constitution requires the Assembly to be immediately convened upon a state of exception declaration. Human rights organizations have filed acción de protección suits against specific emergency measures. The Court has distinguished between legitimate security responses and measures that permanently suspend rights. International human rights standards on derogation from rights in emergencies apply.
laws.penalty: N/A — constitutional review; emergency measures found unconstitutional must be immediately suspended
exceptions: Certain non-derogable rights (prohibition of torture, habeas corpus) cannot be suspended even in emergency
Court review happens expedited in first 72 hours after declaration
International human rights treaty obligations continue even during emergencies

quiz.q: What has Ecuador's Constitutional Court done regarding Noboa's 2024 anti-cartel emergency declarations?
options: Upheld the core military deployment while requiring additional oversight measures
Referred the matter to the IACtHR
quiz.explanation: Ecuador's Constitutional Court reviewed Noboa's 2024 anti-cartel emergency declarations, upholding the core military deployment against cartels while requiring additional oversight measures — exercising its constitutional review power.

laws.title: Disability Rights and Inclusion Law
laws.subtitle: Ecuador's Organic Law on Disability
laws.fullDescription: Ecuador's Organic Law on Disability (Ley Orgánica de Discapacidades, 2012) was a significant reform championed by Lenin Moreno (then-Vice President, himself in a wheelchair following a gunshot injury) before he became president. The law mandates 4% quota for disabled workers in companies with 25+ employees, provides social security benefits, and requires accessibility in public buildings. The CONADIS (National Council for Disability Equality) coordinates policy. Ecuador has a relatively high reported disability rate partly due to conflict-related injuries and medical causes including childhood vaccine-preventable conditions in older generations. Inclusive education provisions are in the education law.
laws.penalty: Fines for employers below the 4% hiring quota; accessibility violations subject to sanctions
exceptions: Small businesses with fewer than 25 employees exempt from quota
Certain physically demanding jobs may qualify for exemption on safety grounds
Disability is broadly defined including physical, mental, and sensory impairments

quiz.q: Who championed Ecuador's Organic Law on Disability before becoming president?
quiz.explanation: Lenin Moreno, who later became Ecuador's president (2017–2021), championed the Organic Law on Disability while serving as Vice President — himself in a wheelchair following a gunshot injury, making the issue personally significant.

laws.title: Whistleblower Protection and Anti-Corruption
laws.subtitle: Ecuador's protection for those reporting government wrongdoing
laws.fullDescription: Ecuador's Organic Law of Citizen Participation and Social Control provides some framework for whistleblowers who report corruption. Witnesses in Odebrecht-related cases received protection. However, formal whistleblower protection legislation is limited — Ecuador lacks a dedicated, comprehensive whistleblower protection law. Journalists who exposed corruption under Correa faced prosecution rather than protection. The Consejo de Participación Ciudadana y Control Social (CPCCS) receives corruption complaints. Civil society organizations provide informal support to whistleblowers. The security crisis has created additional risks for those reporting cartel infiltration of institutions.
laws.penalty: N/A — protection framework; retaliation against witnesses is a criminal offense
exceptions: Witnesses in formal criminal investigations receive prosecutor protection
Anonymous complaints to the Contraloría can be filed without identification
Civil society organizations provide informal support outside formal legal framework

quiz.q: What body in Ecuador receives corruption complaints from citizens?
options: Consejo de Participación Ciudadana y Control Social (CPCCS)
quiz.explanation: Ecuador's Consejo de Participación Ciudadana y Control Social (CPCCS) receives corruption complaints from citizens as part of its civic oversight mandate — though Ecuador lacks a dedicated comprehensive whistleblower protection law.

laws.title: Sustainable Development and SDG Framework
laws.subtitle: Ecuador's implementation of sustainable development goals
laws.fullDescription: Ecuador incorporated Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) into its National Development Plan (Plan Nacional de Desarrollo). The SENPLADES and later the Secretaría Nacional de Planificación coordinates SDG implementation. Ecuador has made progress on poverty reduction (extreme poverty fell from 37% in 2006 to 8% in 2014, though recovering from COVID impacts), education access, and maternal health. Environmental SDGs face tension with extraction-dependent economic model. The 'Ecuador Verde' (Green Ecuador) initiative promoted sustainable production. International environmental financing through GEF, GCF, and bilateral donors supplements domestic capacity.
laws.penalty: N/A — development planning framework
exceptions: Private sector SDG commitments are voluntary rather than legally required
Local governments develop their own SDG localization plans
Indigenous development plans may use alternative well-being frameworks including Buen Vivir

quiz.q: To what level did Ecuador reduce extreme poverty between 2006 and 2014?
quiz.explanation: Ecuador reduced extreme poverty from 37% in 2006 to 8% in 2014 under the Correa government's social investment programs — though poverty rates increased again after the economic downturn and COVID-19 impacts.

laws.title: Civil Registry and Identity Documents
laws.subtitle: Ecuador's civil identification and documentation system
laws.fullDescription: Ecuador's Registro Civil administers national identity documents (cédula de ciudadanía), birth certificates, marriage and divorce records, and passports. The cédula is required for virtually all government services, financial transactions, and voting. Ecuador has invested in biometric identification systems. Birth registration coverage is high in urban areas but still reaches only ~95% in remote indigenous areas. Undocumented indigenous births — particularly of communities with traditional birth practices — can create legal statelessness risks. The Registro Civil has been modernized to allow online services. Political controversies around voter rolls and identity have arisen in election contexts.
laws.penalty: Administrative fines for failure to register vital events within legal timeframes
exceptions: UNHCR assists refugees with documentation in absence of nationality documents
Extended timelines for birth registration in remote indigenous areas
Emergency documentation for disaster-displaced persons

quiz.q: What identity document is required for virtually all government services and financial transactions in Ecuador?
quiz.explanation: Ecuador's cédula de ciudadanía (national identity card) is required for virtually all government services, financial transactions, and voting — making civil registration critical for access to rights and services.

laws.title: Restorative Justice and Alternative Dispute Resolution
laws.subtitle: Ecuador's framework for non-criminal resolution of disputes
laws.fullDescription: Ecuador's legal system incorporates restorative justice mechanisms and alternative dispute resolution (ADR). The Organic Code of the Judiciary (COFJ) encourages mediation and arbitration for civil disputes. Community justice (justicia comunitaria) is recognized for internal community matters. Mediation centers (centros de mediación) operate throughout the country, including at courts. Environmental disputes have used mediation with the Rights of Nature providing a framework. Family disputes are routinely mediated before court proceedings. The arbitration framework is important for commercial and investment disputes, with Ecuador arbitration law aligned with international standards (UNCITRAL).
laws.penalty: N/A — ADR framework; voluntary participation; court enforcement of mediated agreements
exceptions: Criminal cases generally cannot be mediated out of the formal system (except minor offenses)
Family violence cases specifically excluded from standard mediation — separate protection order process
International investment disputes may go to ICSID arbitration under BIT provisions

quiz.q: What international arbitration rules does Ecuador's commercial arbitration align with?
quiz.explanation: Ecuador's commercial arbitration framework is aligned with UNCITRAL (UN Commission on International Trade Law) rules — the standard international arbitration framework used for cross-border commercial and investment disputes.

laws.title: Environmental Rights and Constitutional Protections
laws.subtitle: Ecuador's comprehensive environmental constitutional framework
laws.fullDescription: Ecuador's 2008 Constitution contains the most extensive environmental protections of any constitution — including Rights of Nature, the right of citizens to live in a healthy environment, the precautionary principle, prohibition of nuclear and chemical weapons, protection of biodiversity, food sovereignty, and water as a human right. The Constitutional Court has enforced these rights in numerous cases. The Rights of Nature have been invoked against mining, oil extraction, road construction, and urban development projects. Ecuador has an Acción de Protección de la Naturaleza allowing any citizen to defend nature in court. Despite the strong legal framework, implementation faces constant tension with economic development needs.
laws.penalty: Injunctions and remediation orders for environmental rights violations; criminal prosecution for serious environmental crimes
exceptions: National interest projects may proceed with enhanced environmental mitigation
Existing legal activities with prior permits continue with review for Rights of Nature
Scientific research in protected areas with appropriate authorization

quiz.q: What unique legal mechanism allows any Ecuadorian citizen to defend nature in court?
options: Acción de Protección de la Naturaleza
quiz.explanation: Ecuador's Acción de Protección de la Naturaleza allows any citizen — not just directly affected parties — to defend nature's constitutional rights in court, a unique mechanism stemming from the 2008 constitution's Rights of Nature provisions.

laws.title: Mining Law and Large-Scale Mining Projects
laws.subtitle: Ecuador's emerging large-scale mining sector
laws.fullDescription: Ecuador has significant mineral resources including copper, gold, and silver. The 2009 Mining Law opened the sector to large-scale mining under government oversight. The Mirador copper mine (operated by Chinese company ECSA) became Ecuador's first major open-pit metal mine. The Fruta del Norte gold mine (Lundin Gold) is another significant project. Mining has generated conflict with indigenous communities and environmental defenders — Ecuador has one of the highest rates of criminalization of land defenders in Latin America. The Ministry of Mining manages licensing. Mining royalties and taxes are significant revenue potential. The government balances environmental concerns with fiscal needs.
laws.penalty: Criminal prosecution for illegal mining; environmental violations subject to fines and remediation orders
exceptions: Small-scale artisanal mining in designated areas has simplified licensing
Environmental impact assessments required for all large projects
Communities must be consulted before permits issued in or near their territories

quiz.q: Which company operates Ecuador's first major open-pit copper mine (Mirador)?
quiz.explanation: The Mirador copper mine — Ecuador's first major open-pit metal mine — is operated by ECSA (Empresa Ecuatoriana de Cobre S.A.), a subsidiary of Chinese companies, reflecting Ecuador's significant Chinese mining investment.

laws.title: Cultural Diversity and Afro-Indigenous Arts
laws.subtitle: Ecuador's cultural expression and heritage promotion
laws.fullDescription: Ecuador's remarkable cultural diversity — encompassing 14 indigenous nationalities, Afro-Ecuadorian communities, Montubio (coastal mestizo) culture, and national mestizo traditions — is reflected in rich artistic traditions. The Ministerio de Cultura promotes Ecuadorian cinema (Ecuador has produced internationally recognized films), music (pasillo is the national music, alongside cumbia, sanjuanito, and Afro-Ecuadorian chontaduro rhythms), visual arts, and literature. The Casa de la Cultura Ecuatoriana supports cultural production nationally. Interculturality is a constitutional value. Public funding for arts is distributed through cultural funds. Indigenous festivals (Inti Raymi, Pawkar Raymi) are protected and promoted.
laws.penalty: N/A — cultural promotion framework; copyright protections apply to cultural works
exceptions: Indigenous traditional knowledge and cultural expressions have special protection from commercial exploitation
Religious cultural events have separate authorization procedures
International cultural co-productions facilitated through cultural ministry agreements

quiz.q: What is Ecuador's national music genre?
quiz.explanation: Pasillo is Ecuador's national music genre — a romantic musical form with Spanish, indigenous, and African influences that developed in the 19th and 20th centuries and is recognized as a symbol of Ecuadorian cultural identity.

laws.title: National Police Reform and Accountability
laws.subtitle: Ecuador's police oversight after corruption scandals
laws.fullDescription: Ecuador's Policía Nacional has faced significant corruption challenges — officers have been documented facilitating cartel operations, extorting businesses, and engaging in drug trafficking themselves. The 2021–2024 security crisis revealed deep police institutional failures. Internal Affairs and the Defensoría del Pueblo investigate complaints. Police reform programs supported by UNODC and bilateral partners aim to professionalize the force. Police leaders have been replaced multiple times during the security crisis. Human rights organizations document excessive force against protesters. The intersection of cartel corruption and police creates a systemic accountability challenge.
laws.penalty: Dismissal and criminal prosecution for corrupt officers; fines and criminal liability for excessive force
exceptions: Military forces deployed alongside police have different accountability mechanisms
Undercover operations have special authorization rules
International cooperation operations may involve shared jurisdiction

quiz.q: What international body has supported Ecuador's police professionalization programs?
options: UNODC (UN Office on Drugs and Crime)
quiz.explanation: UNODC (UN Office on Drugs and Crime) has supported Ecuador's police reform and professionalization programs — part of international efforts to strengthen Ecuador's institutions in the face of cartel corruption and the security crisis.

laws.title: Sustainable Agriculture and Agroecology Law
laws.subtitle: Ecuador's promotion of sustainable farming practices
laws.fullDescription: Ecuador's food sovereignty framework promotes agroecology — sustainable farming that minimizes chemical inputs, preserves biodiversity, and maintains traditional seed varieties. The National Seed System protects farmers' rights to save, use, and exchange traditional seeds — a provision that conflicts with intellectual property rights of seed companies. The Organic Agriculture Regulation covers certification and marketing. Agricultural biodiversity centers in different climate zones maintain genetic resources. Community seed banks preserve indigenous varieties. Ecuador's diverse microclimates support enormous agricultural biodiversity — from coastal cacao to highland potato varieties to Amazon fruits. The Ministry of Agriculture promotes sustainable practices.
laws.penalty: Fines for seed monopoly violations; criminal prosecution for theft of traditional seed knowledge
exceptions: Public universities may conduct research with commercial seed varieties
Certified organic farms may use non-organic seeds if organic equivalent unavailable
Emergency pest or disease situations may permit temporary use of prohibited inputs

quiz.q: What right do Ecuador's food sovereignty laws protect for farmers regarding seeds?
options: Right to patent new seed varieties
Right to save, use, and exchange traditional seeds
Right to receive government seed subsidies
Right to veto commercial seed introductions
quiz.explanation: Ecuador's National Seed System and food sovereignty framework protect farmers' rights to save, use, and exchange traditional seeds — a provision that creates tension with intellectual property rights of commercial seed companies.

laws.title: Anticorruption Bodies — CPCCS and Contraloría
laws.subtitle: Ecuador's multi-body anti-corruption institutional framework
laws.fullDescription: Ecuador's anti-corruption architecture includes the Contraloría General (supreme audit institution), the Consejo de Participación Ciudadana y Control Social (CPCCS — citizen participation council), the Superintendencias (sector regulators), and the Fiscalía (criminal prosecution). The CPCCS was created by the 2008 constitution to appoint oversight body leaders independently of political branches. A 2018 referendum changed CPCCS selection from citizen vote to professional committee selection after criticism that citizen-elected members were politically connected. The Contraloría audits government spending and can issue pre-approvals for large contracts. Inter-institutional coordination has improved but duplication of effort remains.
laws.penalty: N/A — oversight institutions; findings referred to Fiscalía for prosecution
exceptions: Military spending audited by specialized military audit body
Intelligence spending subject to classified audit procedures
International organization funds may be audited by donor country standards

quiz.q: What change did Ecuador's 2018 referendum make to the CPCCS?
options: Changed selection from citizen vote to professional committee
Made it a directly elected body
quiz.explanation: Ecuador's 2018 referendum changed the CPCCS selection method from citizen vote to professional committee — a reform responding to criticism that citizen-elected members had political connections undermining the body's independence.

laws.title: Environmental Defenders — Criminalization Risk
laws.subtitle: Ecuador's threats against land and environmental defenders
laws.fullDescription: Ecuador has one of the highest rates of criminalization of environmental and land defenders in Latin America. Indigenous leaders, community activists, and environmental organizations opposing mining, oil, and infrastructure projects face criminal charges — typically sabotaje y terrorismo (sabotage and terrorism), illicit association, and obstruction. Global Witness has documented murders of environmental defenders in Ecuador. Defenders report surveillance, threats, and physical attacks. Despite constitutional Rights of Nature and indigenous consultation rights, those who enforce these rights in practice face systematic repression. The UN Special Rapporteur on Environmental Defenders has called on Ecuador to protect activists.
laws.penalty: N/A — activists face prosecution under existing criminal provisions rather than specific law targeting them
exceptions: UN Special Rapporteur communications can pressure government to drop charges
IACHR precautionary measures provide some protection for named defenders at risk
Academic and international organization staff have more institutional protection

quiz.q: What criminal charges are most commonly used against environmental defenders in Ecuador?
options: Sabotaje y terrorismo (sabotage and terrorism) and illicit association
quiz.explanation: Environmental defenders in Ecuador are most commonly charged with sabotaje y terrorismo (sabotage and terrorism) and illicit association — charges that carry heavy penalties and are widely criticized as being used to criminalize legitimate protest and rights defense.

laws.title: Digital Economy and Fintech Regulation
laws.subtitle: Ecuador's emerging digital financial sector
laws.fullDescription: Ecuador's digital economy has grown rapidly — mobile internet penetration exceeds 70%. The SRI (tax authority) operates an electronic invoicing system. Digital payments including mobile wallets and online banking are increasingly regulated by the Superintendencia de Bancos and Junta de Regulación Financiera. Fintech companies operate in a regulatory sandbox framework introduced in 2020. Cryptocurrency is not legal tender but is not banned for personal use. The security crisis created demand for digital payment systems as cash handling became dangerous in some areas. E-commerce accelerated during COVID-19 lockdowns. Digital signature and electronic contract frameworks are established.
laws.penalty: Fines for unlicensed financial services; criminal prosecution for digital financial fraud
exceptions: Fintech regulatory sandbox allows innovation with lighter compliance initially
Personal crypto holdings not regulated like securities
Micro-enterprise digital payments under threshold exempt from full AML requirements

quiz.q: What useful system does Ecuador's SRI tax authority operate for business compliance?
quiz.explanation: Ecuador's SRI (Internal Revenue Service) operates a mandatory electronic invoicing system that businesses must use — both improving tax compliance and creating digital records of commercial transactions.

laws.title: Femicide Investigation Protocol
laws.subtitle: Ecuador's specialized investigative approach to femicide
laws.fullDescription: Following recognition that femicide cases were poorly investigated as generic homicides, Ecuador developed the Femicide Investigation Protocol — a specialized framework for the Fiscalía and National Police. The protocol requires documenting evidence of gender-based motivation, relationship to perpetrator, prior violence history, and vulnerability factors. Specialized forensic teams and prosecutors handle femicide cases. The protocol aims to improve conviction rates and ensure that femicide is prosecuted as the specific crime (not reduced to 'passion crime' or homicide). NGOs including ALDEA and Fundación Lunita Lunera monitor femicide cases and support families. Data collection on femicide was inconsistent before 2019.
laws.penalty: Femicide: 22–26 years; enhanced if victim was pregnant, disabled, or killed in front of children
exceptions: Cases where gender motivation is disputed may begin as homicide investigation and be reclassified
Femicide by persons under 18 subject to juvenile justice with different penalties
International cases involving dual nationality victims may involve coordination with foreign prosecutors

quiz.q: What was the problem with femicide investigation before specialized protocols were developed in Ecuador?
options: Cases were poorly investigated as generic homicides
quiz.explanation: Before specialized protocols, femicide cases in Ecuador were poorly investigated as generic homicides — failing to document gender-based motivation and reducing cases to lesser charges — which the Femicide Investigation Protocol specifically addresses.

laws.title: Pharmaceutical Biodiversity and Bioprospecting Law
laws.subtitle: Ecuador's regulation of access to genetic resources
laws.fullDescription: Ecuador's extraordinary biodiversity — particularly in the Amazon and cloud forests — makes it a target for bioprospecting (searching for commercially valuable compounds). The Nagoya Protocol (access and benefit sharing) was ratified by Ecuador. The Biodiversity Law requires prior informed consent from communities and benefit-sharing agreements for access to traditional knowledge and genetic resources. Pharmaceutical, cosmetic, and agricultural companies must negotiate agreements with the Ministry of Environment and affected communities. Ecuador has documented cases of biopiracy — unauthorized use of indigenous plants. The traditional knowledge of Amazonian indigenous peoples has commercial value that legal frameworks attempt to protect.
laws.penalty: Fines and criminal prosecution for bioprospecting without authorization; benefit-sharing violations actionable in court
exceptions: Academic research for non-commercial purposes with community consent has simplified procedures
Traditional use by indigenous communities of their own knowledge is not restricted
Regulated commercial agreements with proper consent and benefit-sharing are legal

quiz.q: What international agreement did Ecuador ratify to protect against biopiracy of genetic resources?
options: Nagoya Protocol on access and benefit sharing
quiz.explanation: Ecuador ratified the Nagoya Protocol on access and benefit sharing, requiring prior informed consent and benefit-sharing agreements for access to genetic resources and traditional knowledge — addressing concerns about biopiracy of Amazonian biodiversity.

laws.title: Ecuador's 2023 Referendum — Yasuní and Drug Vote
laws.subtitle: Citizens' direct role in key environmental and security decisions
laws.fullDescription: Ecuador's August 2023 elections included a referendum with eight questions alongside presidential/legislative elections. Two results were globally significant: 59% of Ecuadorians voted to halt oil drilling in the Yasuní-ITT block (Block 43) within Yasuní National Park — a historic conservation vote with global implications for Amazon protection. Separately, voters also approved measures strengthening security responses to drug trafficking. The Yasuní vote required ending oil extraction within one year — affecting approximately 12% of Ecuador's oil production. This direct democracy outcome demonstrated the power of Ecuador's citizen initiative mechanisms and the public's willingness to accept economic costs for environmental protection.
laws.penalty: N/A — referendum result; government must implement by law; failure to comply challengeable before Constitutional Court
exceptions: Oil company contracts require negotiated termination with compensation
Oil workers receive transition support under social protection programs
Timeline for withdrawal subject to technical and safety requirements

quiz.q: What percentage of Ecuadorians voted to halt Yasuní drilling in the 2023 referendum?
quiz.explanation: 59% of Ecuadorians voted to halt oil drilling in the Yasuní-ITT block in the August 2023 referendum — a historic conservation decision that will affect approximately 12% of Ecuador's oil production.
